case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Utah Supreme Court affirmed the court of appeals' disavowal of the 'almost automatically' line of cases and held that the statutory 'strictly necessary' requirement is not a separate third element but a mandatory part of the best-interest inquiry, so a juvenile court must expressly consider feasible alternatives to termination.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Utah framework for terminating parental rights: grounds alone never suffice, and the court must find termination strictly necessary from the child's point of view.
key_cases.quote: as part of that inquiry, a court must specifically address whether termination is strictly necessary to promote the child's welfare and best interest

key_cases.holding: The court disavowed its 'almost automatically' line of cases, held that the statutory 'strictly necessary' requirement is analyzed as part of the best-interest element rather than as a separate third element, held that best interest must therefore be applied more thoroughly and independently than earlier cases suggested, and remanded for reconsideration — the decision the Utah Supreme Court affirmed in 2020.
key_cases.relevance: It is the working exposition of Utah's termination test that practitioners cite alongside the Supreme Court's affirmance, and it is the decision that ended the inference that statutory grounds carry best interest almost automatically.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that courts should analyze the "strictly necessary" language as part of the "best interest" element of our historical test

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the court of appeals, holding that In re B.T.B. created no new substantive right, that appellate courts may not graft a 'materially better' test onto the statutory strictly-necessary standard, and that the court of appeals exceeded appropriate appellate review by reweighing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the current Utah formulation of the strictly-necessary/best-interest test and rejects judicially added glosses on the statute.
key_cases.quote: the court erred by applying the "materially better" standard instead of the relevant statutory language

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may sever the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, and that New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: It is the federal constitutional floor — clear and convincing evidence — that Utah's termination statute and In re G.D. implement.
key_cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

key_cases.holding: The Court declined to raise the burden of proof for termination from clear and convincing evidence to beyond a reasonable doubt, and held the juvenile court adequately conducted the strictly-necessary analysis, including considering the grandmother as a kinship alternative.
key_cases.relevance: It settles that clear and convincing evidence, not proof beyond a reasonable doubt, is the Utah standard for terminating parental rights.
key_cases.quote: The juvenile court did not err in declining to apply the "beyond a reasonable doubt" standard of proof.

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the court of appeals and reinstated the termination order, holding that the juvenile court's best-interest determination — including its rejection of permanent guardianship with the grandmother in favor of adoption — was supported by the evidence and not against its clear weight.
key_cases.relevance: It is the most recent Utah Supreme Court application of the strictly-necessary standard and confirms the deference owed to a juvenile court's termination decision.
key_cases.quote: Because the juvenile court's best interest determination was supported by the evidence, we reverse.

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21, only while the juvenile court orders DCFS to keep serving the young adult (Utah Code 80-1-102(56)(b)(i); 78A-6-120(1)(a)). A young adult who is 18 or older but younger than 21 and in DCFS custody on abuse, neglect, or dependency grounds may petition the juvenile court to be removed from division custody, and the court reviews that petition within 14 days; if removed, the young adult may petition within 90 days to re-enter division custody, and the juvenile court shall order the division to take custody (Utah Code 80-3-503)
